The student files with the Registrar’s Office a statement of approval by the dean of the college/school and the chair of the department in which she or he wishes to complete the second degree;

The student’s major for the second degree is taken in a subject matter field other than the one in which she or he was awarded the first degree; and furthermore,

The credit-hour requirements for the major leading to the second baccalaureate degree are those specified in the current catalog and will have been earned after the awarding of the first baccalaureate degree.

In addition, the following regulations apply:

A minimum of 32 credit hours toward the second baccalaureate degree must be completed in residence at the University of Guam.

Students holding a baccalaureate degree from other U.S. accredited four-year colleges and universities or foreign equivalent may attempt a second baccalaureate degree at the University of Guam provided they meet the relevant requirements listed above.

The Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education (WICHE) is a regional organization created by the Western Regional Education Compact and adopted in the 1950s by Western states. WICHE was created to facilitate resource sharing among the higher education systems of the West. Helping students gain affordable access to higher education is one of its objectives.

The Western Undergraduate Exchange (WUE) is coordinated by WICHE. Students enrolled through WUE pay up to 150% of the enrolling institution’s resident undergraduate tuition. To qualify, applicants must demonstrate residency in a WICHE member state and must be admitted to a WUE-eligible major at UOG.

WICHE's member states include 15 Western states and member U.S. Pacific Territories and Freely Associated States (currently, the Republic of Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Republic of Paulau and Guam). WICHE’s 15 member states are: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming.

item.title: Tåotao Tritons | More than a Picture: Chance Douglas and the Stories Behind the Lens
item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) Tåotao Tritons | More than a Picture: Chance Douglas and the Stories Behind the Lens
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons | More than a Picture: Chance Douglas and the Stories Behind the Lens

Chance Douglas, a ’16 and ’18 UOG alumnus and Financial Aid Office Program and Outreach Coordinator

At the age of two years old, disposable cameras were already among Chance Douglas’s favorite things to play with. Since then, he’s learned that some of the most meaningful moments happen in a fraction of a second: a triumphant smile on a graduate’s face, a family gathered for a cultural celebration, or loved ones’ tearful joy during a wedding. The two-time University of Guam alumnus and current Program and Outreach Coordinator at the Financial Aid Office did not anticipate that a childhood hobby would eventually grow into something much more significant.

Douglas’s fascination with taking pictures grew with each passing year. As he got older, relatives upgraded him from disposable cameras to more long-lasting equipment, though developing the film remained an expense. For his birthdays, he would sometimes give the film rolls to his grandmother and ask her to have the photos printed as his gifts. His older sister became his willing—and sometimes unwilling—model. Douglas would do her makeup, direct her poses, and experiment with different setups. His childhood is filled with photographs of others, but ironically, he admits he only has just a few of himself.

“I was always behind the camera, so I don’t have pictures,” he says. “I have pictures of people, but not myself.”

It was not until after Douglas earned his bachelor’s degree that he was able to afford what he considered his first “real” camera and began taking photography more seriously. Through trial and error, studying the work of other photographers, and watching online tutorials from what he calls “YouTube University,” Douglas explored and absorbed different artistic techniques and editing styles.

Portraits became his primary focus. What started with friends and maternity shoots expanded into senior portraits, proms, weddings, conferences, cultural ceremonies, and other milestones. As he shared his work online, word spread, particularly within his home community of Palau, and that’s when he realized that photography could be more than a hobby.

Still, Douglas’s approach has been less about creating a heavily edited image and more about highlighting what’s already there. He gravitates toward a natural look and tries to make the people in front of his camera comfortable enough to show it.

“Everyone looks good in pictures,” he says. “It’s just how you get them to feel it.” For Douglas, that often means joking with clients, getting to know them, or simply giving them time to relax.

As Douglas developed his skills and gained more experience, he began to realize the weight a single image could carry.

One particular instance drastically changed the way he viewed his work. While at a high school function, Douglas snapped a shot of one of the students. Within hours of the event, the student passed away in a fatal accident, and suddenly, a picture that had been one of many from an otherwise normal evening became something irreplaceable.

The experience reinforced for Douglas that photography is ultimately the preservation of memories. A graduation, anniversary, or family gathering may pass in a matter of hours, but the photographs from those celebrations allow people to return to pieces of those moments long after they are gone.

It is no surprise, then, that Douglas has grown fond of candid photography. At a wedding, for example, he may momentarily shift his focus from the main ceremony toward the reactions happening around it, like an auntie wiping away a tear, a flower girl peeking shyly from behind one of the bridesmaids, or guests laughing at a story shared about the couple.

These moments unfold for only a few seconds, and Douglas recognizes they cannot be simply staged again. “You can never say, ‘Start crying. Can you cry again?’” he jokes.

Chance Douglas uploads pictures on his photography Instagram page

Douglas’s understanding of the moments worth capturing is also shaped by his Palauan identity and culture.

Among his favorite events to photograph is the Palauan first-childbirth ceremony, known as Omengat. The occasion brings together not only the mother, child, and partner, but also extended families and clans, with cultural details unfolding throughout the celebration.

Douglas explains that someone unfamiliar with the ceremony might naturally focus solely on the mother while overlooking a person, object, or interaction in the periphery that carries cultural significance. Because he understands the nuances, he can anticipate and preserve them alongside the larger celebration.

“I love the Palauan community because I can tell this story,” Douglas says. “I understand the significance, the importance of the details.”

Chance Douglas reviews pictures on his camera

As photography continues to evolve, Douglas wants to evolve with it. He recently invested in new equipment and hopes to eventually expand into videography. One project he hopes to pursue hits close to home.

Douglas wants to document Palauan elders, including family members of his own, and preserve their stories in short videos that the younger generation can easily watch and understand.

For a culture in which generations of history and knowledge have been carried largely through oral traditions, he recognizes that some stories became increasingly vulnerable as elders grow older. He hopes videos can provide another way of carrying those voices forward.

From disposable cameras and rolls of undeveloped films to the celebrations and stories he hopes to preserve next, Douglas continues to find himself capturing moments, one frame at a time.

item.title: UOG Valedictorian Chia-Chia Hsieh's Journey of Growth, Service, and Academic Excellence
item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) UOG Valedictorian Chia-Chia Hsieh’s Journey of Growth, Service, and Academic Excellence
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

UOG Valedictorian Chia-Chia Hsieh’s Journey of Growth, Service, and Academic Excellence

Most students measure the road to college graduation in years, but Chia-Chia Hsieh can also measure her educational journey in miles—over 1,700 miles, to be more precise.

Crossing time zones and international waters, Hsieh came to Guam from Taiwan when she was 16 years old. It was her first time living away from home, and she had to adjust to a new environment, a different culture, and an unfamiliar language.

Adapting to the changes took time, but they helped Hsieh become a dedicated, resilient student. She ultimately found her way to the University of Guam, where she pursued a Chemistry-Biology dual degree and earned the honor of being named the class valedictorian for Fañomnåkan (Spring) 2026.

While high academic achievement has undoubtedly been a highlight for Hsieh, the support she has received from the Triton community and the personal and professional growth she has experienced have been equally memorable and impactful.

In the first few years after moving to Guam, there were moments where Hsieh felt lonely and unsure about whether she fit in. It was at UOG that she began to develop a stronger sense of belonging.

“What made UOG special was never only the classrooms or laboratories, but the people,” Hsieh says.

Classmates became sources of encouragement and support through hectic semesters. Professors shared their knowledge readily, often offering assistance even outside of class time. Advisors and mentors provided guidance on everything from internship opportunities to future career prospects.

The meaningful relationships Hsieh forged at UOG helped transform uncertainty into confidence.

“So many people encouraged me during times when I doubted myself,” Hsieh says. “Those experiences taught me the importance of kindness, empathy, and community support, especially for students studying far away from home.”

In addition to working on the core requirements of her major, Hsieh was active in research, teaching assistantships, leadership activities, and community service, all of which strengthened her professional growth.

Hsieh had the opportunity to attend a research internship at Academia Sinica, one of the leading academic institutions in Taiwan, where she studied plant heat acclimation and abiotic stress memory. Her interest in scientific inquiry and innovation grew even more after a research project she conducted on the antioxidant properties of breadfruit leaves through UOG’s Agriculture and Life Sciences Laboratory. The project helped Hsieh realize how science intersected with culture, traditional knowledge, and public well-being.

“That experience changed the way I viewed research,” Hsieh shares. “I learned that research is not only about generating data, but also about understanding people, respecting local knowledge, and finding ways science can serve communities more meaningfully.”

As Hsieh prepares to attend the University of Michigan College of Pharmacy to pursue a Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) degree, she brings with her a passion to give back, especially through advocacy for equitable healthcare access in underserved and island communities.

“Living and studying in Guam taught me the importance of compassionate, community-centered care and showed me how meaningful it can be to support the communities that support you in return,” Hsieh says.

Hsieh’s dedication to service is also deeply personal. Inspired by her younger brother, who is on the autism spectrum, she has gained broader perspectives on the challenges that individuals and families may face when navigating healthcare systems, as well as the importance of empathy, patience, and communication.

The learning does not end for Hsieh, but even as she leaves UOG, she hopes the institution’s values of Ina, Deskubre, Setbe continue to guide her. Whether in the next stage of her journey or in the distant future, Hsieh is motivated to make a difference in the lives of others.

item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) Tåotao Tritons: Acts of Adornment: Elizabeth M. Rutun and the Craft of Lei-Making
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons: Acts of Adornment: Elizabeth M. Rutun and the Craft of Lei-Making

Professor Elizabeth M. Rutun, a ’18 UOG alumna and Instructor of English

Amidst the sea of black regalia customary at every University of Guam commencement, vibrant pops of color exist in the form of leis. Whether haloes of fuchsia bougainvillea sitting atop the heads of beaming graduates or cords of golden orchids hanging gracefully from their necks, there is never a shortage of these celebratory symbols. More often than not, a fair number of these adornments were crafted by Professor Elizabeth Midil Rutun, hereby referred to as Midil, a 2018 UOG alumna and Instructor of English who imbues both care and intention in every lei she makes.

Long before Midil was making leis for special occasions like graduations, she was a young girl in Yap with a penchant for walking around the village, picking flowers from people’s yards—and getting scolded for it.

“You're not supposed to because every parcel of land belongs to somebody, so it's like you're picking someone's property, and even if it's a flower and I'm a kid, I would always get in trouble,” Midil recalls.

Elizabeth Rutun prepares to cut a stem of orchids

“But then my mom said, ‘You know, if you're going to take people's stuff, you better not take it for no good reason.’”

She began learning how to make leis by watching family members like her older sister. Soon, she was being asked to make them for the tourists who would visit the island on guided tours.

“The leis looked so, so bad,” Midil admits with a laugh, “but the tourists were really impressed by them and would give me 10, 20 bucks.”

Through time, practice, and trial and error, Midil developed her style, along with an acute understanding of how there is always room to improve her skills. Feedback from other lei makers has made such learning experiences possible, and even if the critiques sometimes sting, Midil takes them as valuable opportunities to see her work through others’ eyes.

The Yapese refer to leis, whether they are worn around the neck or as headpieces, as nunuw, the literal translation meaning “adornment.”

Elizabeth Rutun holds up a lei she made recently for Mother’s Day

Midil takes this description to heart in how she approaches her creations, especially since moving to Guam in 2016 and making leis for local audiences.

“The idea is the lei isn't supposed to be the star of the show. In the Yapese way of using them and making them, they're supposed to hide the flaws of the person while illuminating their best parts,” she says.

Midil factors in specifics such as the wearer’s personality, facial features, and skin complexion to create a final piece that truly highlights the person. If she is unable to get this information, other details are just as useful. The event or occasion in which the lei will be worn, as well as the relationship between the giver and receiver of the lei help inform the creative process.

While most local requests prioritize the leis’ aesthetics, Midil makes it a point to also honor their deeper meaning, which has become a lesson for her in how leis function in different contexts.

“You have an art that you’re now taking to another place, and we’re looking at the same thing from different angles,” Midil says.

Elizabeth Rutun works on braiding together a lei

Another aspect of lei-making in which Midil has gained substantial knowledge is the flowers themselves. As expected, color is an important feature to consider, with Midil’s understanding influenced by the Yapese concept of colors being classified as either “alive” or “dead.”

“Usually, brighter colors are ‘alive.’ So, for example, you can have two pink hues. One’s pigment is more complex or saturated, so we describe it as ‘alive.’ The other has less pigment or saturation, making it a ‘dead’ color,” she explains.

When applied to leis, a flower’s color, along with its shape and texture, helps influence whether it enhances the wearer’s features, so Midil pays close attention to such details.

Beyond knowing the characteristics of physical appearance, Midil is also cognizant of flowers’ temperaments—the best time to pick them, how well certain flowers hold up in humid or air-conditioned spaces and for how long, how quickly petals begin to wilt or turn brown.

This knowledge, gained through years of experience and careful observation, helps Midil create leis that are not only visually striking, but sturdy and long-lasting as well.

A decade into making leis in Guam, Midil receives a steady stream of orders throughout the year for various occasions, from birthdays and school events to traditional cultural performances and welcome ceremonies for visiting dignitaries. Understandably, Mother’s Day and graduation season are particularly busy times.

A holiday for which there is a surprising demand for leis? “Thanksgiving,” Midil reveals. “I’ve had people gift my leis to their dinner guests.”

Even with a consistent demand for her work, Midil continues to evolve in her art, experimenting with styles, techniques, and the types of plants she uses. She hopes people can be more open to the possibilities of what leis can look like, such as those made with ferns and even pineapple skin.

Occasionally, Midil receives unique requests that push her creativity further, such as a recent one to incorporate a katupat, or a CHamoru woven rice pouch, into the design. These kinds of project opportunities are what keep the craft engaging and worthwhile, challenging Midil to use her skills to create something deeply personal and symbolic.

“You’re not just making a lei. You're trying to capture an idea through a lei, and I think, like all forms of art, it has so much more meaning when it does that,” Midil says.

Elizabeth Rutun points out ixora, one of the many flowers she uses for making leis
